title: Early inputs for 2027–2030 strategic plan
subtitle: Resident survey on affordability and growth, UN Sustainable Development Goals review, and a closed session on four matters.
overview: Council held a special meeting to begin work on the 2027–2030 strategic plan. No decisions were needed on the plan itself. Council heard two early research inputs and was asked which themes staff should explore further.

A resident satisfaction survey, presented by an outside research firm, found satisfaction with City services is high and above comparable municipalities and national results. Affordability and housing were the top concerns. The main gap is between satisfaction today and confidence that services will hold up as the city grows. Satisfaction was lowest among residents in midlife. A University of Waterloo review of how City plans align with the UN Sustainable Development Goals found strong alignment overall, with gaps in equity, inclusion and policy frameworks.

The one motion of substance authorized a closed session after the public meeting, covering four matters: a personal matter, a potential land disposition, negotiations, and legal advice. The minutes report no outcomes from it. Staff will return to Council in August with more input, and public engagement begins in June. Councillors can send further ideas to staff in the coming days.

decisions.detail: Council authorized a closed meeting after the special meeting to consider a personal matter, a potential land disposition, a negotiations position, and two solicitor-client privilege matters {{vote:m1}}.

debate: Councillors asked how much survey results reflect Region of Waterloo issues, such as regional taxes, water supply and waste collection changes, rather than City services. The researcher said the survey used the word 'city' but residents likely blur the two, and it could not be separated.

Several councillors wanted more detail: results by ward, raw responses, open-ended comments, and follow-up on bylaw enforcement dissatisfaction. The researcher said ward-level samples are small and carry a high margin of error. The firm agreed to share open-ended comments and a longer detailed report.

On taxes and services, the survey showed a split. A plurality favoured holding taxes even if services are cut, and more respondents favoured user fees. A delegate from Compass Kitchener said that was surprising and wanted a closer look at the reasons. One councillor noted the survey could not show which services residents would trade off.

On the sustainable development goals review, councillors questioned whether alignment scores overstate the City's role in areas like water, climate and health that the Region or other governments control. They also asked whether alignment is less useful than measured outcomes. The presenter said the scores measure commitments in City documents, not results, and invited feedback on the targets.
